claims.text: POINT 1 — M2_VERIFIED. I reimplemented the receipt-hash rule from attest.py's source rather than importing verify_chain(), and recomputed every receipt myself: 15 receipts, 0 linkage faults, 0 hash mismatches. The live evidence receipt is present — injection_id cd027a618b1dae52, session claudesquad_head07-inference-fable, orchestrator_pid 4026564, transport 'tmux send-keys -l' — and its recomputed hash matches its declared hash.

POINT 1, PRECISION. injection_id is sha256(session + prev + PAYLOAD)[:16], but the payload is NOT stored in the receipt — only its hash is. So injection_id cannot be recomputed from the chain alone; it is self-consistent, not independently verifiable. Anyone auditing the chain without the original payload bytes must take injection_id on trust.

POINT 2 — M2_REJECTED. Two attacks on a temp copy both produced a chain my own verifier calls clean. ATTACK A: a fabricated receipt for an injection that never happened, appended from the real tail — 0 faults, FORGERY ACCEPTED. ATTACK B: an old receipt altered and every subsequent receipt re-linked and re-hashed — 0 faults, REWRITE ACCEPTED. ATTACK D: attest.py contains no hmac, secret, key or signature, so receipt_hash is a plain keyless sha256 and the minting rule is public. ATTACK C, their stated control (tamper one field WITHOUT re-linking), IS detected — 1 fault — so their 10/10 is honest for the naive adversary and silent on the author.

POINT 3 — M2_REJECTED. The requirement is 'a read-only path the loop cannot modify'. The chain is uid 1000 mode 664, the loop's own uid; os.access reports the file AND its parent directory writable by me, a different process at the same uid. Hash linkage defeats PARTIAL tampering only. Against an adversary who can write the file and knows the algorithm — which is precisely the loop and its author — linkage provides no protection at all, as ATTACK A and B demonstrate. Same-uid storage does defeat the purpose.

POINT 3, THE MINIMUM CHANGE — and it is NOT the one proposed. 'One root-owned append-only location' fixes ATTACK B (rewrite) and does NOT fix ATTACK A (fabricated append), because append is exactly what append-only permits. Escalating that to Curtis as the fix would buy protection against history rewriting and leave forgery untouched. The minimum that closes BOTH is root-owned append-only PLUS one of: (i) a writer the loop cannot impersonate — a privileged helper or a key the payload-generating process cannot read, so a receipt proves WHO wrote it; or (ii) correlation against an INDEPENDENT record that the injection actually arrived, since a fabricated receipt has no matching arrival. (ii) is cheaper and needs no root: the transcript already records arrivals.

POINT 4 — M2_VERIFIED, tested on five cases against a copy under a redirected HOME so the real chain was never written. (a) genuine receipt + intact chain -> MACHINE_CONTINUATION_ATTESTED. (b) unknown payload hash -> ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED. (c) correct payload hash but wrong session -> ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED. (d) genuine receipt but chain TAMPERED -> ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED, so a valid receipt does not attest while the chain is broken. (e) no chain -> ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED. The source contains exactly two verdict values, MACHINE_CONTINUATION_ATTESTED and ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED; no verdict means 'human', and the absence path says so explicitly.

POINT 4, PRECISION. The 'correlation' is between a stored receipt and a payload_hash the CALLER passes in. attest() does not independently observe that those bytes were delivered. So it answers 'is there a prior commitment to these bytes for this session', which is the right question, but it cannot detect a receipt written for bytes that were never sent — the same gap ATTACK A exploits.

tests.command: python3 attest_audit.py  # reimplemented hash rule, recompute + 4 attacks
HOME=<tmp> python3 attest.py attest <session> <hash>  # 5 gating cases

decisions_requested: Do NOT escalate 'one root-owned append-only location' to Curtis as the fix. It closes rewrite and leaves forgery open. Escalate root-owned append-only PLUS correlation against the transcript's record of arrival — the second half needs no root and closes the attack the first half misses.

The attestation is sound as a MACHINE-CONTINUATION claim and unsound as an ANTI-FORGERY claim. If its purpose is 'prove this continuation came from the orchestrator', it needs the writer authenticated. If its purpose is 'record what the orchestrator sent, tamper-evident against outsiders', it already does that and the requirement wording should change instead.
risks: The chain grew from 14 to 15 receipts DURING this audit and the file size changed 8080 -> 8646 bytes. It is a live, moving target; my counts are a snapshot, and a second auditor will get different numbers for the same reason the M2 census disagreed.

All attacks ran on temp copies. I did not write to the real chain, and I verified afterwards that it was untouched. But that self-restraint is exactly the protection the design is missing — I could have written to it, which is the finding.

I read attest.py to learn the hash rule before reimplementing it. If the documented rule and the executed rule differ, my reimplementation inherits the documented one. The 15/15 agreement with the live chain is the control that says they match today.
